solution.concept_anchor: Article 37 non-justiciability versus enforceability
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because students conflate 'non-justiciable' with 'having no legal effect whatsoever,' ignoring DPSPs' interpretive role.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Article 37 explicitly labels DPSPs 'non-justiciable,' so courts cannot be directly petitioned to enforce them.
Eliminate option (b): 'Non-justiciable' does not mean legally irrelevant — DPSPs guide statutory interpretation and determine reasonableness of FR restrictions.
Eliminate option (c): DPSPs are not enforceable in the same manner as FRs under Article 32; the distinction lies in direct vs. indirect effect.
Retain option (d): The precise legal meaning of Article 37 is that DPSPs are binding on the state as governance obligations but courts cannot compel their implementation through writ jurisdiction.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students often treat 'non-justiciable' as synonymous with 'no legal force at all.' The trap here is the assumed equivalence between unenforceability in courts and total legal irrelevance. Article 37 itself calls DPSPs 'fundamental to the governance of the country,' signalling their interpretive weight. Courts regularly use DPSPs to give meaning to 'public interest,' 'reasonableness,' and the substantive content of Article 21 — making DPSPs indirectly operative even though no writ lies for their direct enforcement.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 37 declares that DPSPs, though not enforceable by any court, are 'fundamental in the governance of the country' and the state is duty-bound to apply them in making laws. The critical distinction is between direct justiciability and legal relevance.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Courts cannot entertain petitions to directly enforce a DPSP, which is the core meaning of non-justiciability.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Saying DPSPs have 'no legal effect' overstates the non-justiciability clause; they retain interpretive power.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: DPSPs are not enforceable in the same way FRs are under Article 32 — this conflates the two categories.
• Option (d) — Correct: Non-justiciability means no direct judicial enforcement, but DPSPs remain binding governance obligations and guide courts in interpreting laws and FRs.

Value Addition:
• Ambedkar described DPSPs as 'instruments of instruction' to future governments.
• Courts apply DPSPs to determine whether a restriction on Article 19 is 'reasonable.'
• The non-justiciability of DPSPs parallels that of Fundamental Duties under Article 51A.

concepts_used: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) — The First Flashpoint
First Constitutional Amendment (1951): Legislative Response to Champakam

solution.concept_anchor: Champakam Dorairajan case and First Amendment link

statement_analysis.statement: In Champakam Dorairajan (1951), the Supreme Court held that Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles when the two conflict.
statement_analysis.reason: This was the first explicit SC ruling establishing FR supremacy; Article 46 (promoting weaker sections) could not override Article 15(1) non-discrimination.

statement_analysis.statement: The First Constitutional Amendment (1951) added Article 15(3) to overcome the limitation identified in the Champakam Dorairajan ruling.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 15(3) existed before the First Amendment and enables special provisions for women and children. The First Amendment added Article 15(4) for socially and educationally backward classes.

statement_analysis.statement: The Ninth Schedule was introduced through the First Constitutional Amendment to protect land reform laws from Fundamental Rights challenges.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 31-B and the Ninth Schedule were both products of the First Amendment (1951), shielding specified land reform statutes from FR invalidation.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) appears correct because students recall '15(3)' and 'women' and may associate the First Amendment with empowering backward classes generally, without distinguishing clause numbers.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Champakam is indeed the first case establishing FR supremacy over DPSPs — correct.
Scrutinise Statement 2: Article 15(3) pre-existed the First Amendment (it was part of the original Constitution for women); the First Amendment added Article 15(4) — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3: The Ninth Schedule (Article 31-B) was indeed inserted by the First Amendment — correct.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct, pointing to option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The most dangerous distractor here is the confusion between Article 15(3) and Article 15(4). Article 15(3) — enabling special provisions for women and children — was part of the original Constitution. It is Article 15(4) that was inserted by the First Amendment specifically to respond to Champakam and allow reservations for backward classes. A student who recalls that the First Amendment 'added a clause to Article 15' may incorrectly select the option that includes Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Champakam Dorairajan (1951) was the Supreme Court's first definitive statement that Fundamental Rights, being justiciable, must prevail over DPSPs in case of irreconcilable conflict. Parliament responded within months through the First Constitutional Amendment.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The SC explicitly held that Article 46 (a DPSP) cannot override Article 15(1)'s bar on discrimination.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 15(3) — empowering special provisions for women — already existed in the original Constitution. The First Amendment added Article 15(4) for backward classes.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Ninth Schedule, created by Article 31-B through the First Amendment, was designed to immunise land reform laws from FR-based challenges.

Value Addition:
• The First Amendment is widely regarded as the prototype of Parliament amending FRs to give effect to DPSPs.
• Article 31-B creates a legal fiction: laws in the Ninth Schedule are deemed valid notwithstanding anything in Part III.
• The Champakam precedent motivated five subsequent property-related amendments over the next three decades.

solution.concept_anchor: 44th Amendment property right demotion to Article 300A

statement_analysis.statement: The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) deleted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31, making the right to property a legal right under Article 300A.
statement_analysis.reason: This is precisely what the 44th Amendment did — property moved from Part III to Part XII as a statutory/legal right, not a fundamental right.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 300A, being part of Part XII, can be enforced through a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 32 enforces only Fundamental Rights listed in Part III. Article 300A (Part XII) is not a FR and can only be enforced via High Court writ jurisdiction under Article 226.

statement_analysis.statement: After the 44th Amendment, laws affecting property rights still require justification under Article 19(5) grounds to be constitutionally valid.
statement_analysis.reason: Once Article 19(1)(f) was deleted, the Article 19 restriction framework no longer applies to property. Article 300A only requires that deprivation occur under legal authority.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) appears correct because students recall Article 32 as the constitutional remedy for rights violations without checking whether Article 300A qualifies as a Fundamental Right.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is factually accurate — the 44th Amendment deleted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 and shifted property to Article 300A in Part XII.
Statement 2 is incorrect — Article 32 jurisdiction is confined to Fundamental Rights in Part III; Article 300A lies in Part XII and is enforceable only via Article 226 in High Courts.
Statement 3 is incorrect — deletion of Article 19(1)(f) removes property from Article 19's framework; Article 300A requires only legal authority for deprivation, not Article 19 justification.
Statements 2 and 3 are both incorrect, matching option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 2 is the assumption that any constitutionally recognised right can be enforced through Article 32. Article 32 is the 'right to constitutional remedies' only for Part III Fundamental Rights. Article 300A is in Part XII — a different part — making it a legal/constitutional right but not a Fundamental Right. Consequently, only the High Court's broader writ power under Article 226 can address its violation, not the Supreme Court's Article 32 jurisdiction.
solution.final_explanation:
The 44th Amendment (1978) is a landmark in the DPSP–FR conflict because it resolved the property rights battleground by removing property from the Fundamental Rights chapter entirely.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 were deleted; Article 300A in Part XII now provides that no person shall be deprived of property except by authority of law.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 32 is available only for Part III Fundamental Rights. Article 300A, residing in Part XII, is not a FR — violations must be addressed via Article 226 (High Court).
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Article 19 grounds framework (clauses 2–6) no longer applies to property after deletion of Article 19(1)(f). The sole test under Article 300A is existence of legal authority.

Value Addition:
• Post-44th Amendment, DPSPs on land distribution (Articles 39(b) and 39(c)) face significantly weaker constitutional resistance.
• Article 300A is often called a 'statutory right' — it requires an Act of Parliament or Legislature, not merely an executive order.
• This amendment followed the Kesavananda Bharati framework — Parliament can curtail FRs if basic structure is preserved.

Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) — The Grand Reconciliation
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) — Defining the Balance

solution.concept_anchor: Article 31C scope after Minerva Mills

statement_analysis.statement: Article 31C, as originally inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971), shielded laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
statement_analysis.reason: The original Article 31C specifically covered Articles 39(b) and (c), protecting such laws from Articles 14 and 19 challenges.

statement_analysis.statement: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court upheld the entire Article 31C as inserted by the 25th Amendment without striking down any part of it.
statement_analysis.reason: The Court upheld the protection granted by Article 31C but struck down the clause that made a Parliamentary declaration that a law implements 39(b)/(c) non-justiciable.

statement_analysis.statement: The 42nd Amendment (1976) extended Article 31C's protection to all Directive Principles, and this extension was upheld in Minerva Mills (1980).
statement_analysis.reason: Minerva Mills (1980) explicitly struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs as a violation of the basic structure.

statement_analysis.statement: After Minerva Mills (1980), Article 31C continues to operate but only shields laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c), not all DPSPs.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-Minerva Mills, the original scope of Article 31C — limited to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) — survives; the extended scope stands invalidated.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' tempts students who correctly identify statements 1, 3, and 4 as correct but miss that statement 2 is incorrect because Kesavananda did partly strike down Article 31C.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Article 31C as originally enacted covered only Articles 39(b) and (c).
Statement 2 is incorrect — Kesavananda struck down the non-justiciability clause of Article 31C while upholding its protective shield.
Statement 3 is incorrect — The 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C to ALL DPSPs was struck down in Minerva Mills, not upheld.
Statement 4 is correct — Post-Minerva Mills, Article 31C survives but only in its original limited scope covering Articles 39(b) and (c).
Two statements (1 and 4) are correct, selecting option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Two traps operate simultaneously. First, students who know Kesavananda upheld Article 31C in general may assume it was upheld entirely — missing the partial invalidation of the non-justiciability clause. Second, students often confuse the 42nd Amendment's extension being struck down with Article 31C itself being struck down. Neither is true: Article 31C survived but in truncated form. A candidate selecting 'Only three' likely accepts Statement 3 as correct, which is the classic extension fallacy.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 31C represents Parliament's most direct attempt to subordinate certain Fundamental Rights to specific DPSPs. Understanding its evolving scope is crucial.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 25th Amendment's Article 31C shielded laws advancing Articles 39(b)/(c) from Articles 14 and 19 challenges.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Kesavananda upheld Article 31C's protective effect but struck down the clause preventing judicial examination of whether a law genuinely implements 39(b)/(c).
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Minerva Mills (1980) struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs, holding that the balance between Part III and Part IV is itself basic structure.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Only the original narrow scope (Articles 39(b) and (c)) of Article 31C remains operative.

Value Addition:
• Minerva Mills framed FRs and DPSPs as 'two wheels of a chariot' — neither can be sacrificed.
• The non-justiciability clause struck in Kesavananda would have allowed Parliament to certify any law as DPSP-implementing without judicial check.
• Article 31C does not shield laws from Article 21 challenges — only Articles 14 and 19.

solution.concept_anchor: Ninth Schedule judicial review — pre and post Kesavananda
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) swaps the ruling in I.R. Coelho with Waman Rao, exploiting the fact that both cases deal with Ninth Schedule immunity and students may not distinguish their precise holdings.
elimination_logic: Identify A: Waman Rao (1981) established the April 24, 1973 cutoff — laws before that date are fully protected; this matches description 3.
Identify B: I.R. Coelho (2007) held that post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws are open to basic structure review including FR (Articles 14, 19, 21) scrutiny — matches description 1.
Identify C: The basic structure doctrine, established in Kesavananda Bharati, is the constitutional standard applied to post-1973 Ninth Schedule additions — matches description 4.
Identify D: April 24, 1973 is the date Kesavananda was decided and serves as the judicial cutoff for Ninth Schedule immunity — matches description 2.
Correct combination is A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Waman Rao–I.R. Coelho confusion is a classic UPSC trap. Both cases address Ninth Schedule immunity, but their precise holdings differ: Waman Rao established the 1973 cutoff date, while I.R. Coelho (a nine-judge bench) strengthened the position that even post-1973 laws in the Ninth Schedule can be struck down if they abridge core FRs forming part of basic structure. Students who know both cases exist but not their specific contributions often swap the holdings.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ninth Schedule's constitutional immunity is not absolute — its scope has been progressively defined by landmark cases.

Correct Matching:
• A (Waman Rao, 1981) → 3: Established that laws added to the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973 (Kesavananda date) enjoy complete immunity from FR challenge.
• B (I.R. Coelho, 2007) → 1: A nine-judge bench held that post-1973 Ninth Schedule additions are open to challenge if they damage basic structure, including core FRs under Articles 14, 19, 21.
• C (Basic Structure Doctrine) → 4: The test for post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws is not the schedule itself but whether the law violates the basic structure.
• D (April 24, 1973) → 2: This date marks the pronouncement of Kesavananda Bharati and serves as the constitutional dividing line for Ninth Schedule immunity.

Value Addition:
• I.R. Coelho involved the Tamil Nadu Backward Classes Act (1993) placed in the Ninth Schedule after 1973.
• The Ninth Schedule currently contains over 280 entries — mainly land reform and reservation laws.
• Waman Rao is the bridge between Kesavananda's theoretical doctrine and the practical protection afforded to pre-1973 land reform statutes.

solution.concept_anchor: Kesavananda reconciliation formula — FRs not subordinate to DPSPs
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify both A and R as true often assume the causal connection automatically, without scrutinising whether R logically explains A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. Kesavananda held that Parliament can amend FRs to implement DPSPs provided the basic structure is preserved; it did not establish DPSP supremacy.

Step 2: Is R correct? — No. Minerva Mills described FRs and DPSPs as 'two wheels of a chariot,' not Kesavananda Bharati. Moreover, R overstates by implying DPSPs are categorically superior — Minerva Mills said balance is the key, not DPSP dominance.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer must be (c).
Correct option is (c): A is correct, R is incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is attributing the 'two wheels of a chariot' metaphor to Kesavananda Bharati when it is actually from Minerva Mills (1980). Additionally, the Reason suggests DPSPs are superior to FRs — which is precisely what Kesavananda rejected. The case held that Parliament has power to amend FRs to balance them with DPSPs within basic structure limits, not that DPSPs override FRs. A student reading both A and R casually may accept R as a general truth about constitutional harmony without checking the precise case attribution.
solution.final_explanation:
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) is the most consequential judgment on the DPSP–FR relationship. Understanding its precise holding is critical.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: Kesavananda held that Parliament has the constituent power to amend Fundamental Rights to give effect to DPSPs, but cannot destroy the basic structure of the Constitution in doing so. The case expressly denied that DPSPs are superior to FRs.
• Reason (R) — Incorrect: The 'two wheels of a chariot' metaphor was articulated in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), not in Kesavananda. Furthermore, R implies DPSP superiority, which contradicts both Kesavananda and Minerva Mills, both of which insisted on balance rather than hierarchy.
• Since A is correct but R contains a factual attribution error and a substantive misstatement, option (c) is correct.

Value Addition:
• Kesavananda was heard by a 13-judge bench — the largest constitutional bench in Indian judicial history.
• The basic structure doctrine is now the constitutional ceiling on Parliament's amending power under Article 368.
• Minerva Mills (1980) built on Kesavananda to declare that the harmony between Part III and Part IV is itself a basic structure element.

solution.concept_anchor: 86th Amendment Article 21A and Article 45 age-range transition
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who recall the Unni Krishnan case and the 86th Amendment may place the former after the latter, reversing the sequence.
elimination_logic: Unni Krishnan v. State of AP (1993) was the first step — deriving the right to education from Article 21 read with Article 45 DPSP; it precedes any constitutional amendment.
The 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) inserted Article 21A, converting the right to education into a justiciable FR — this followed the Unni Krishnan judgment.
The Right to Education Act (2009) was the legislative implementation of Article 21A inserted in 2002 — it is the last in the sequence.
Correct order: Unni Krishnan (1993) → 86th Amendment (2002) → RTE Act (2009) → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is inverting the judicial and legislative steps. Students who recall that 'Unni Krishnan led to the right to education' may not be certain whether the judgment preceded the amendment or followed a failed legislative attempt. The 2009 RTE Act is sometimes confused with the 2002 amendment, and students may also invert the amendment-Act sequence.
solution.final_explanation:
The journey of the right to education from a DPSP to a Fundamental Right unfolded in three stages:

• Unni Krishnan v. State of AP (1993): The Supreme Court read Article 21 (right to life) with Article 45 (DPSP on free education) to derive a fundamental right to free education up to age 14. This was judicial interpolation before any constitutional amendment.
• 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002): Formally inserted Article 21A, making free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 a Fundamental Right. Simultaneously, Article 45 DPSP was amended to shift its focus to early childhood care for children below 6 years.
• Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act (2009): The enabling legislation operationalising Article 21A, enacted seven years after the amendment.

Wrong orderings in the options either place the RTE Act before the amendment or Unni Krishnan after the amendment — both chronologically impossible.

Value Addition:
• Article 21A covers 6–14 years; Article 45 DPSP now covers below-6 early childhood care — the age-ranges are a frequent exam trap.
• The 86th Amendment also added Article 51A(k) as a Fundamental Duty — parents must provide educational opportunities to children aged 6–14.
• Unni Krishnan is also the source of the 'capitation fee' prohibition for private educational institutions.

concepts_used: Article 44 (Uniform Civil Code) vs. Articles 25–28 (Religious Freedom)

solution.concept_anchor: Article 44 UCC vs Article 25 — regulation of secular religious activities
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Article 25 guarantees freedom of religion may assume any UCC legislation directly violates it, without appreciating the secular-activities exception in Article 25(2)(b).
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Article 26 protects management of religious affairs by religious denominations — not the applicable provision for state regulation of personal laws.

Eliminate option (b): Article 25(1) protects religious practice but Article 25(2)(b) explicitly permits the state to make laws providing for social welfare and reform, including regulation of secular activities associated with religion.
Eliminate option (c): Article 29 protects cultural and educational rights of minorities — not directly the constitutional gateway for personal law reform.

Retain option (d): Article 25(2)(b) is the constitutional gateway that allows the state to legislate on secular activities associated with religious practice, which is how UCC proponents argue that personal law reform can coexist with religious freedom.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students conflate the right to freedom of religion under Article 25(1) with its qualifications. Article 25(2)(b) explicitly carves out the state's power to regulate or restrict secular activities associated with religious practice. Parliament can enact a UCC by invoking this gateway — the constitutional argument is that personal laws governing marriage, inheritance, and succession are secular in character even if shaped by religion. Students who treat Article 25 as an absolute bar miss this nuance.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional tension between Article 44 (UCC as a DPSP) and Articles 25–28 (religious freedom as FRs) is best understood through the Article 25(2)(b) gateway.

A state legislature proposes a uniform family law code for all citizens. Religious organisations challenge it as violating their community's personal laws protected under Article 25.

• Option (a) — Article 26: Protects religious denominations' right to manage their own affairs — relevant to internal religious governance, not personal law reform by the state.
• Option (b) — Article 25(1) as absolute bar: Incorrect. Article 25 itself contains exceptions; clause (2)(b) permits state regulation of secular activities associated with religion.
• Option (c) — Article 29: Deals with protection of minority cultural and language rights — not the primary constitutional interface for personal law reform.
• Option (d) — Correct: Article 25(2)(b) allows the state to regulate secular activities associated with religion, including personal laws on marriage and succession. This is the constitutional basis reconciling Article 44 with Article 25.

Value Addition:
• Shah Bano (1985) invoked Article 44, but Parliament enacted the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986 to overrule it.
• Sarla Mudgal (1995) and John Vallamattom (2003) further urged Parliamentary action on UCC.
• The Supreme Court has consistently held that Article 44 is not self-executing — it requires legislative action.

Right to Health and Environmental DPSPs vs. Article 21

solution.concept_anchor: DPSPs used to expand Article 21 via judicial interpretation
solution.strong_distractor: b — Olga Tellis is sometimes associated with housing rights rather than livelihood, leading students to doubt its Article 21 connection and misidentify it as the odd one.
elimination_logic: Unni Krishnan (1993) expanded Article 21 using Article 45 DPSP to derive the right to education — clear Article 21 expansion via DPSP.
Olga Tellis (1985) expanded Article 21 using Article 39(a) DPSP to derive the right to livelihood — clear Article 21 expansion via DPSP.
Subhash Kumar (1991) expanded Article 21 using Article 48A DPSP to derive the right to pollution-free water and air — clear Article 21 expansion via DPSP.
Champakam Dorairajan (1951) established FR supremacy over DPSPs — it is NOT an example of DPSPs expanding FRs; it is the opposite: FRs prevailing over DPSPs.
Champakam Dorairajan is the odd one out — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is that all four cases involve DPSPs and FRs, making the surface connection seem uniform. However, Champakam Dorairajan is structurally the opposite of the other three: while Unni Krishnan, Olga Tellis, and Subhash Kumar used DPSPs to enrich Article 21, Champakam used Article 15 (FR) to strike down a DPSP-motivated government order. A student who recalls only that all four are DPSP-FR cases will struggle to identify the structural difference.
solution.final_explanation:
Three of these cases share a common pattern: DPSPs were used as interpretive tools to expand the substantive content of Article 21.

• Unni Krishnan v. State of AP (1993): Article 45 (DPSP — education) read with Article 21 to derive the right to education.
• Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985): Article 39(a) (DPSP — adequate means of livelihood) read with Article 21 to recognise the right to livelihood.
• Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991): Article 48A (DPSP — environment protection) read with Article 21 to establish the right to pollution-free water and air.
• Champakam Dorairajan (1951): Does NOT fit this pattern. It held that a state government order implementing Article 46 (DPSP) violated Article 15(1) (FR) — i.e., the FR prevailed over the DPSP, not the reverse.

Value Addition:
• The tripartite framework of Articles 48A + 51A(g) + 21 creates overlapping environmental obligations for the state and citizens.
• Article 21's 'right to life' has been the most expansive constitutional provision through judicial interpretation.
• Olga Tellis is also known as the 'pavement dwellers case' — eviction without alternative shelter violated Article 21.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 15(5) and minority institution exception under Article 30

statement_analysis.statement: The 93rd Constitutional Amendment (2005) added Article 15(5), enabling the state to make special provisions for reservation in private unaided educational institutions.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 15(5) was inserted to overcome the PA Inamdar ruling and expressly authorises reservation in private unaided institutions for backward classes and SCs/STs.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 15(5) applies uniformly to all private unaided educational institutions, including those established and administered by religious and linguistic minorities.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 15(5) explicitly excludes minority educational institutions protected under Article 30(1) — minority unaided institutions are exempt from reservation mandates under this provision.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the 93rd Amendment expanded reservation to private unaided institutions may accept Statement 2 as a natural extension without recalling the Article 30 exception.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — the 93rd Amendment inserted Article 15(5) specifically to enable reservation in private unaided institutions after the PA Inamdar ruling.
Statement 2 is incorrect — Article 15(5) contains an explicit proviso exempting minority educational institutions under Article 30(1) from its scope.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap operates on Statement 2: students who know Article 15(5) enables reservation in private unaided institutions may assume it applies universally. The constitutional text of Article 15(5) contains a proviso that carves out minority educational institutions established under Article 30(1), recognising that imposing state-mandated reservations on minority institutions would undermine their fundamental right to administer their own educational establishments.
solution.final_explanation:
The 93rd Amendment was Parliament's direct response to PA Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005), in which the Supreme Court held that the state cannot impose reservation on unaided private institutions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 15(5) was inserted to explicitly authorise reservation in private unaided educational institutions for backward classes, SCs, and STs.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 15(5) contains a proviso expressly excluding minority educational institutions protected under Article 30(1). Minority communities retain the right under Article 30 to administer their educational institutions, and the reservation mandate does not reach them.

Value Addition:
• TMA Pai Foundation (2002) established a three-tier hierarchy: minority unaided > non-minority unaided > aided institutions in terms of permissible state regulation.
• The PA Inamdar ruling prompted the 93rd Amendment within the same year (2005).
• Article 15(5) is a classic example of Parliament amending FRs to accommodate DPSP goals — here, Articles 46 and 41 (right to education for weaker sections).

concepts_used: Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) as a Bridge Between FRs and DPSPs

solution.concept_anchor: Fundamental Duties placement in Part IVA not Part IV
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who associate Fundamental Duties with DPSPs as 'non-justiciable state obligations' often incorrectly place FDs in Part IV alongside DPSPs.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): DPSPs are in Part IV — Fundamental Duties were added separately and are NOT in Part IV.
Eliminate option (c): Part III contains Fundamental Rights — Fundamental Duties are not FRs.
Eliminate option (d): Part V deals with the Union executive and legislature — unrelated to duties.
Retain option (b): Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA (Article 51A), inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) as a distinct part between Part IV (DPSPs) and Part V.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The near-identical naming of 'Part IV' (DPSPs) and 'Part IVA' (Fundamental Duties) is a classic UPSC precision trap. Because Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable like DPSPs, and were added in the same amendment era, students conflate the two. Part IVA is a separate, distinct part of the Constitution created specifically for Fundamental Duties.
solution.final_explanation:
The 42nd Amendment (1976) made two major additions to the constitutional structure.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Part IV is already occupied by Directive Principles of State Policy (Articles 36–51). Fundamental Duties are not in Part IV.
• Option (b) — Correct: Fundamental Duties under Article 51A are housed in Part IVA — a new part inserted between Part IV (DPSPs) and Part V (the Union), created specifically by the 42nd Amendment.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Part III is the chapter on Fundamental Rights. Fundamental Duties are legally distinct from Fundamental Rights and occupy a different part.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Part V covers the Union — executive, Parliament, and related provisions. It has no connection with citizen duties.

Value Addition:
• India currently has 11 Fundamental Duties — the 11th was added by the 86th Amendment (2002) making parents duty-bound to provide education to children aged 6–14.
• Fundamental Duties, like DPSPs, are non-justiciable — courts cannot directly enforce them.
• Courts use Article 51A to assess the reasonableness of FR restrictions in cases involving environmental violations and national integrity.

concepts_used: 42nd Amendment (1976) — The High-Water Mark of DPSP Supremacy

solution.concept_anchor: 42nd Amendment — what was struck down vs what survived
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who recall that Minerva Mills struck down the 42nd Amendment's DPSP-related changes may conclude that all 42nd Amendment additions were invalidated, making option (c) seem correct.
elimination_logic: Examine option (a): The 42nd Amendment extended Article 31C to all DPSPs — this is correct; Minerva Mills struck down this extension. The pair is accurately stated.
Examine option (b): The 42nd Amendment added Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) — this is correct; but Fundamental Duties were NOT struck down by Minerva Mills. The second element of the pair is false.
Examine option (c): Minerva Mills struck down the extension of Article 31C, not Article 31C itself — the pair misstates what was struck down.
Examine option (d): Article 31D (anti-national activities) was added by the 42nd Amendment but was repealed by the 44th Amendment, not struck down by Minerva Mills.
Only option (a) presents a correctly matched pair — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 42nd Amendment was a sweeping legislative exercise — it added Fundamental Duties, extended Article 31C, added Article 31D, and inserted new DPSPs. Minerva Mills struck down the Article 31C extension but left Fundamental Duties and the new DPSPs intact. Students who conflate 'struck down by Minerva Mills' with 'all 42nd Amendment additions' will incorrectly reject option (a) or accept option (b) or (c).
solution.final_explanation:
The 42nd Amendment (1976) was the most ambitious attempt to tilt the constitutional balance toward DPSP supremacy.

• Option (a) — Correct: The 42nd Amendment extended Article 31C's protection to all DPSPs; this extension was struck down in Minerva Mills (1980) as violating the basic structure. The pair is correctly matched.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The 42nd Amendment did add Article 51A (Fundamental Duties), but Minerva Mills did not strike down Fundamental Duties — they remain valid. The second element is false.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Minerva Mills struck down the extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs, not Article 31C itself. The original Article 31C (covering Articles 39(b)/(c)) survived.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Article 31D was added by the 42nd Amendment but was repealed by the 44th Amendment (1978), not invalidated by any Supreme Court ruling.

Value Addition:
• The 42nd Amendment is nicknamed the 'Mini-Constitution' for the breadth of its changes.
• Fundamental Duties (Part IVA) survived judicial scrutiny and are used to assess reasonableness of FR restrictions.
• The 44th Amendment (1978) reversed several 42nd Amendment changes, including deleting Article 31D.

concepts_used: Articles 14, 19 vs. DPSPs — Doctrine of 'Reasonable Restriction'

solution.concept_anchor: DPSP as reasonable restriction — Article 19 express grounds requirement

statement_analysis.statement: Courts may invoke a Directive Principle alone as a sufficient constitutional ground to uphold a restriction on a right guaranteed under Article 19(1).
statement_analysis.reason: A DPSP cannot by itself justify an Article 19 restriction — the restriction must fit within the express grounds enumerated in Article 19(2) through 19(6), such as interests of the general public or sovereignty.

statement_analysis.statement: When examining whether a restriction on an Article 19 right is 'reasonable,' courts may consider the extent to which the impugned law advances a Directive Principle.
statement_analysis.reason: Courts read DPSP objectives into terms like 'interests of general public' and 'reasonableness,' using DPSPs to determine whether a restriction is constitutionally justified.

statement_analysis.statement: A law challenged under Article 14 can be sustained if there is an intelligible differentia and rational nexus between the classification and the Directive Principle the law seeks to implement.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 14's equality test (intelligible differentia + rational nexus) can be satisfied where the classification is tied to a legitimate DPSP objective, making the differentiation reasonable.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know DPSPs are used in Article 19 analysis may assume DPSPs alone suffice as constitutional justification, making option (b) (Statement 2 only) seem under-inclusive.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect — a DPSP alone cannot justify an Article 19 restriction; the express grounds in Article 19(2)-(6) remain mandatory.
Statement 2 is correct — DPSPs inform the 'reasonableness' analysis within the express Article 19 grounds.
Statement 3 is correct — under Article 14's two-pronged test, a DPSP objective can supply the rational nexus required for the classification.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 1 is subtle: students who know DPSPs are used in Article 19 analysis may assume they operate as independent constitutional grounds for restriction. In reality, DPSPs cannot expand the closed list of grounds in Article 19(2)–(6). They can only inform how existing grounds (like 'public interest') are interpreted — not substitute for them. This distinction between DPSPs as interpretive aids versus independent restriction grounds is frequently confused.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between DPSPs and Article 19's restriction framework is one of interpretive guidance, not substantive expansion.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 19 restrictions are governed by a closed list of grounds in clauses (2)–(6). A DPSP cannot independently justify a restriction — it must fit within an express ground. DPSPs serve as aids to interpret 'reasonableness' and 'public interest,' not as standalone justifications.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Courts use DPSP goals to assess whether a restriction is 'reasonable' — if a law advances a DPSP objective and fits within an express Article 19 ground, it is more likely to be upheld.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Under Article 14, the rational nexus component of the equality test can be satisfied by demonstrating that a classification serves a DPSP-backed legislative purpose.

Value Addition:
• State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951) used this analytical approach — DPSP-backed prohibition legislation was balanced against Article 19(1)(g) (trade and profession).
• Article 19(6) expressly permits restrictions on the right to trade 'in the interest of the general public' — courts read DPSP objectives into this phrase.
• This interpretive tool avoids the need for constitutional amendment in many cases where DPSPs and FRs appear to conflict.

concepts_used: Harmonious Construction: The Judicial Default Rule

solution.concept_anchor: Harmonious construction as first principle in DPSP–FR conflicts
solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who recall Kesavananda's basic structure doctrine may identify it as the first principle applied, not recognising that harmonious construction precedes basic structure analysis.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): FR supremacy (Champakam rule) is invoked only when harmony between FRs and DPSPs is genuinely impossible — it is not the first step.
Eliminate option (c): Article 31C provides a legislative shield for specific DPSPs — it is a statutory tool, not the courts' default interpretive principle.
Eliminate option (d): The basic structure doctrine applies to constitutional amendments, not to the ordinary interpretive conflict between FRs and DPSPs in legislation.
Retain option (b): Harmonious construction is the judicial default — courts first attempt to read FRs and DPSPs together before declaring an irreconcilable conflict.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students trained on the hierarchy (Champakam → Article 31C → Kesavananda) may jump to the basic structure doctrine as the governing principle of DPSP–FR conflicts. However, the judiciary's first tool is harmonious construction — interpreting both Part III and Part IV together to avoid conflict wherever possible. Conflict resolution mechanisms like FR supremacy or Article 31C are invoked only when harmony is structurally impossible.
solution.final_explanation:
Indian constitutional courts follow a hierarchy of interpretive principles when FRs and DPSPs appear to conflict.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Champakam rule (FR supremacy over DPSPs) is a conflict-resolution rule of last resort, not the starting point of constitutional analysis.
• Option (b) — Correct: Harmonious construction is the default judicial principle — courts strive to read FRs and DPSPs as mutually reinforcing rather than antagonistic. This was affirmed in Pathumma v. State of Kerala (1978) and State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas (1976).
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Article 31C is a Parliamentary instrument providing legislative protection for specific DPSP-implementing laws — it is not the courts' interpretive starting point.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The basic structure doctrine governs the validity of constitutional amendments, not the interpretation of ordinary legislation under DPSP–FR tension.

Value Addition:
• State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas (1976) read Article 16(4) (reservations) harmoniously with Article 16(1) (equality), exemplifying the harmonious construction approach.
• Courts use DPSPs to determine the 'reasonableness' of FR restrictions — a direct application of harmonious construction.
• Only when harmony is structurally impossible does the Champakam FR-supremacy rule come into play.

concepts_used: Article 39(b) & (c): Material Resources Distribution vs. Article 19(1)(g)

solution.concept_anchor: Article 39(b) — judicially contested scope of 'material resources'

statement_analysis.statement: Article 39(b) directs that the material resources of the community shall be distributed to subserve the common good, and this directive is the constitutional basis for nationalisation legislation.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 39(b) provides exactly this directive — it has been consistently used as the constitutional foundation for nationalisation and distributive legislation.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court has authoritatively settled in State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy (1977) that privately owned resources do not qualify as 'material resources of the community' under Article 39(b).
statement_analysis.reason: Ranganatha Reddy produced a split verdict — there was no authoritative settlement. The question of whether private resources fall within 'material resources of the community' remains judicially contested and has been referred to a larger bench.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 39(c), which prevents the concentration of wealth and means of production, forms the constitutional basis for anti-monopoly and competition legislation.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 39(c) specifically addresses concentration of economic power — it is the constitutional directive underlying anti-monopoly laws and competition policy.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who have read about the Ranganatha Reddy case may recall it as a landmark on Article 39(b) and assume it settled the 'private resources' question, making option (a) (Statement 1 only is wrong) appealing.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Article 39(b) is indeed the constitutional basis for nationalisation laws.
Statement 2 is incorrect — Ranganatha Reddy produced only a split verdict; the question remains unresolved and is pending before a larger bench in the Property Owners' Association case.
Statement 3 is correct — Article 39(c) is the basis for anti-monopoly and concentration-of-wealth legislation.

Only Statement 2 is incorrect → option (b) — but checking the option pattern: the question asks which are NOT correct, and the answer choices include options covering different combinations; option (c) states 'Statement 2 only' — verify option letters match.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is presenting the Ranganatha Reddy (1977) split verdict as a settled ruling. Because it is a known landmark case on Article 39(b), students assume it resolved the question. In reality, the split verdict left the issue open — Justice Krishna Iyer's view that private resources can be 'material resources of the community' did not command a majority. The matter was referred to a nine-judge bench in the Property Owners' Association case and remains judicially unsettled.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 39(b) and (c) represent the core economic directives in the DPSP framework and have been the subject of major judicial controversy.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 39(b) mandates distribution of material resources of the community for the common good — it is the constitutional anchor for nationalisation statutes.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Ranganatha Reddy case produced a split bench verdict. No authoritative ruling exists on whether privately owned resources constitute 'material resources of the community.' This question remains before a larger bench (Property Owners' Association v. State of Maharashtra).
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 39(c) targets concentration of wealth — it underpins anti-monopoly legislation and competition policy frameworks.

Value Addition:
• Article 31C (original scope) specifically protects laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from Articles 14 and 19 challenges.
• The unresolved question about private resources under 39(b) has significant implications for future land acquisition and nationalisation law.
• Justice Krishna Iyer's expansive reading of 'material resources' in Ranganatha Reddy remains doctrinally influential even without majority support.

Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) as a Bridge Between FRs and DPSPs

solution.concept_anchor: Tripartite environmental framework Articles 48A, 51A(g), and 21
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who correctly identify both A and R as true may be unsure whether the tripartite framework involving 48A and 51A(g) genuinely explains why pollution-free environment falls under Article 21.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. The right to a pollution-free environment has been held by the Supreme Court (Subhash Kumar, 1991; MC Mehta series) to be part of the right to life under Article 21.

Step 2: Is R correct? — Yes. Articles 48A (state duty to protect environment — DPSP) and 51A(g) (citizen duty to protect environment — Fundamental Duty) together with Article 21 create the tripartite constitutional framework for environmental protection.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. Courts derived the right to a pollution-free environment under Article 21 precisely by reading it with Articles 48A and 51A(g), making the tripartite framework the explanation for A.
All three steps affirmative → correct option is (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Environmental protection in Indian constitutional law rests on three interlocking provisions that courts have synthesised into a unified framework.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: The Supreme Court in Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991) and the MC Mehta series held that the right to live in a pollution-free environment is an integral part of the right to life under Article 21.
• Reason (R) — Correct: Article 48A (a DPSP) imposes a duty on the state to protect and improve the environment. Article 51A(g) (a Fundamental Duty) imposes a corresponding obligation on every citizen. Courts read these together with Article 21 to give environmental rights a constitutional foundation.
• Causal Link: R genuinely explains A — courts derived the environmental dimension of Article 21 by reading it with Articles 48A and 51A(g), making the tripartite framework the direct explanatory cause.

Value Addition:
• Article 48A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) — one of the new DPSPs that survived Minerva Mills.
• Article 51A(g) makes it a duty of every citizen to protect the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers, and wildlife.
• The tripartite framework (48A + 51A(g) + 21) is frequently tested in the context of the Precautionary Principle and Polluter Pays Principle in Indian environmental law.

concepts_used: Property Rights Conflict: Articles 19(1)(f), 31 vs. Land Reform DPSPs
First Constitutional Amendment (1951): Legislative Response to Champakam

solution.concept_anchor: Constitutional amendments curtailing property rights — sequential order
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who remember '17th Amendment' and '25th Amendment' may invert their order, particularly because the 17th Amendment is less prominent in standard notes.
elimination_logic: The First Amendment (1951) added Article 15(4) and the Ninth Schedule — this is the starting point, the earliest amendment.
The Fourth Amendment (1955) widened the scope of the Ninth Schedule and amended Article 31 to restrict compensation for acquired property.
The Seventeenth Amendment (1964) added more land reform laws to the Ninth Schedule and expanded the definition of 'estate' under Article 31A.
The Twenty-Fifth Amendment (1971) inserted Article 31C, shielding laws implementing Articles 39(b)/(c) from Articles 14 and 19.
The Forty-Fourth Amendment (1978) deleted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31, completing the property rights curtailment journey.
Correct sequence: 1st → 4th → 17th → 25th → 44th → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 4th and 17th Amendments are the least-recalled members of the property rights amendment sequence. Students who remember the 1st, 25th, and 44th Amendments may misplace the 4th and 17th. Options are designed to test whether students know the full sequence, not just the landmark endpoints.
solution.final_explanation:
The curtailment of property as a Fundamental Right unfolded through five constitutional amendments spanning nearly three decades.

• First Amendment (1951): Added Article 15(4) and the Ninth Schedule — the legislative response to Champakam; initial protection for land reform laws.
• Fourth Amendment (1955): Widened Ninth Schedule coverage and amended Article 31 to reduce the state's obligation to pay equivalent compensation for acquisition.
• Seventeenth Amendment (1964): Expanded Article 31A by broadening the definition of 'estate' and added more land reform laws to the Ninth Schedule.
• Twenty-Fifth Amendment (1971): Inserted Article 31C — the most direct attempt to shield DPSP-implementing laws from Articles 14 and 19 challenges.
• Forty-Fourth Amendment (1978): Completed the process by deleting Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 entirely, moving property to Article 300A in Part XII.

Value Addition:
• This sequence demonstrates the 'pattern established' by the First Amendment: Parliament amending FRs to accommodate DPSPs.
• The 25th and 42nd Amendments (1971 and 1976) represent the high-water mark of DPSP assertion over FRs.
• Post-44th Amendment, property rights conflicts primarily arise under Articles 300A and 14, not Article 19.

solution.concept_anchor: DPSPs expanding Article 21 — case-provision mapping

statement_analysis.statement: In Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), the Supreme Court derived the right to livelihood from Article 21 read with Article 41 (right to work) as a Directive Principle.
statement_analysis.reason: Olga Tellis read Article 21 with Article 39(a) (adequate means of livelihood for all citizens), not Article 41. Article 41 concerns the right to work, education, and public assistance — a related but distinct DPSP.

statement_analysis.statement: In Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993), the right to free education up to the age of 14 was derived from Article 21 read with Article 45 as a Directive Principle.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the precise derivation in Unni Krishnan — the court read Article 21 with Article 45 (free and compulsory education up to 14 years) to recognise education as a fundamental right.

statement_analysis.statement: The indirect enforceability of Directive Principles through Article 21 means that a DPSP can be directly enforced via a writ petition without any supporting statutory framework.
statement_analysis.reason: DPSPs are not independently enforceable through writ petitions even after their content is read into Article 21. The Article 21 right itself becomes enforceable — the DPSP provides interpretive content, not a standalone writ cause of action.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who correctly reject Statement 1 (wrong DPSP provision) but accept Statement 3 (confusing Article 21 enforceability with DPSP enforceability) will choose (b) rather than (d).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Olga Tellis used Article 39(a), not Article 41 — the entity-swap makes this incorrect.
Statement 2: Unni Krishnan correctly used Article 45 DPSP read with Article 21 — this is correct.
Statement 3: DPSPs remain non-justiciable even when their content informs Article 21; it is the expanded Article 21 right that is enforceable, not the DPSP directly.
Only Statement 2 is correct → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Two traps operate: Statement 1 swaps Article 39(a) with Article 41 — both are DPSPs related to livelihood/work, making the swap subtle. Statement 3 exploits the confusion between 'DPSPs can be read into Article 21' and 'DPSPs become directly enforceable through Article 21.' The latter is incorrect — it is the Article 21 right that gains enforceability; the DPSP itself remains non-justiciable.
solution.final_explanation:
Courts use DPSPs as interpretive lenses to give substantive content to Article 21, but the mechanism operates through Article 21, not independently.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Olga Tellis (1985) derived the right to livelihood from Article 21 read with Article 39(a) (DPSP ensuring adequate means of livelihood for all citizens). Article 41 — which concerns the right to work, education, and public assistance — was not the operative DPSP in this case.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Unni Krishnan (1993) read Article 21 with Article 45 (DPSP on free education up to 14 years) to recognise a fundamental right to free education — the bridge that eventually led to Article 21A.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Even when a DPSP's content is absorbed into Article 21, the DPSP itself does not become directly enforceable. The enforceability flows through Article 21 — the DPSP remains a non-justiciable interpretive input.

Value Addition:
• Article 39(a) ensures citizens have adequate means of livelihood — it is in the 'Gandhian' cluster of DPSPs.
• Article 45 was amended by the 86th Amendment to now focus on early childhood care for children below 6 years.
• The Unni Krishnan ruling also introduced the famous distinction between 'commercial education' and 'non-commercial education' in private institutions.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 21A covers 6–14 years; Article 45 DPSP covers below-6

statement_analysis.statement: Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002), guarantees the right to free and compulsory education to all children between the ages of 6 and 14 years.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 21A precisely covers the age group 6–14 years — this is the constitutional text.

statement_analysis.statement: After the 86th Amendment, Article 45 (Directive Principle) continues to direct the state to provide free and compulsory education to all children up to the age of 14 years.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 45 was simultaneously amended by the 86th Amendment to shift its focus to early childhood care and education for children below 6 years, not up to 14 years — that obligation moved to the Fundamental Right under Article 21A.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who recall that 'Article 45 was about education up to 14 years' may not know that the 86th Amendment also amended Article 45 to change its focus to below-6 years.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Article 21A covers 6–14 years, as explicitly stated in the constitutional text.

Statement 2 is incorrect — the 86th Amendment simultaneously amended Article 45 DPSP to redirect its focus from 'education up to 14 years' to 'early childhood care and education for children below 6 years.'
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students memorise the pre-Amendment Article 45 (education up to 14 years as a DPSP) and may be unaware that the 86th Amendment simultaneously changed Article 45's content. The Amendment was a two-part operation: create Article 21A (FR for 6–14 years) AND amend Article 45 (DPSP now focuses on below-6 early childhood care). Failing to know the second part of this operation leads to accepting Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The 86th Amendment (2002) executed a precise constitutional surgery on the education provisions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 21A mandates free and compulsory education for children in the 6–14 age group as a Fundamental Right, enforceable under Articles 32 and 226.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 86th Amendment did not merely add Article 21A — it simultaneously amended Article 45. The pre-amendment Article 45 directed the state to provide free education up to age 14. Post-amendment, Article 45's focus shifted entirely to early childhood care and education for children below the age of 6 years. The 6–14 mandate migrated to Part III as a FR.

Value Addition:
• The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act (2009) operationalises Article 21A — enacted seven years after the amendment.
• The 86th Amendment also added Article 51A(k) as a Fundamental Duty: parents/guardians must provide educational opportunities to their children aged 6–14.
• The age-range split (below-6 under Article 45 DPSP; 6–14 under Article 21A FR) is one of the most frequently tested precision facts in UPSC Prelims.

solution.concept_anchor: Minerva Mills holdings — what it struck down and affirmed

statement_analysis.statement: Minerva Mills (1980) struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C to all Directive Principles as violating the basic structure.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the primary holding of Minerva Mills — the extension of Article 31C beyond Articles 39(b) and (c) to all DPSPs was invalidated.

statement_analysis.statement: Minerva Mills (1980) held that judicial review over constitutional amendments is not a basic structure element and Parliament can exclude such review.
statement_analysis.reason: Minerva Mills held the opposite — judicial review over constitutional amendments IS a basic structure element; Parliament cannot oust it, and the 42nd Amendment's attempt to do so was struck down.

statement_analysis.statement: Minerva Mills (1980) held that the balance between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV) is itself a feature of the basic structure.
statement_analysis.reason: This is a key affirmative holding — the constitutional harmony between Part III and Part IV cannot be destroyed; maintaining that balance is a basic structure requirement.

statement_analysis.statement: Minerva Mills (1980) overruled Kesavananda Bharati (1973) by holding that Directive Principles are superior to Fundamental Rights in case of conflict.
statement_analysis.reason: Minerva Mills did not overrule Kesavananda — it built upon it. It expressly rejected DPSP supremacy over FRs and reaffirmed the balance between the two as basic structure.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Minerva Mills struck down two 42nd Amendment provisions may guess 'Only three' by miscounting, particularly if they accept Statement 2 or 4 without precise knowledge.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Minerva Mills struck down the 42nd Amendment's Article 31C extension to all DPSPs.
Statement 2 is incorrect — Minerva Mills affirmed judicial review over amendments as basic structure; the 42nd Amendment's attempt to exclude it was struck down.
Statement 3 is correct — The balance between Part III and Part IV is itself a basic structure feature per Minerva Mills.
Statement 4 is incorrect — Minerva Mills followed and built upon Kesavananda; it did not overrule it and explicitly rejected DPSP supremacy.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — 'Only two' → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 is the most dangerous distractor — students who know Minerva Mills elevated DPSP protection may incorrectly assume it also elevated DPSPs above FRs. The case did the opposite: it protected the balance, rejecting any absolute DPSP supremacy. Statement 2 exploits the assumption that a case striking down a constitutional amendment would logically restrict judicial review — in fact, the court expanded its own reviewability.
solution.final_explanation:
Minerva Mills (1980) is the definitive case on the constitutional limits of DPSP supremacy. Its holdings must be understood with precision.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs was struck down — only Articles 39(b) and (c) remain covered.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Minerva Mills affirmatively held that judicial review over constitutional amendments is a basic structure element. It struck down the 42nd Amendment's clause ousting this review.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The balance between FRs (Part III) and DPSPs (Part IV) is a core basic structure element — neither can be sacrificed for the other.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Minerva Mills built on Kesavananda Bharati, reinforcing its basic structure doctrine. It explicitly rejected DPSP superiority over FRs.

Value Addition:
• Minerva Mills coined the 'two wheels of a chariot' metaphor for the FR–DPSP relationship.
• Judicial review of constitutional amendments (as distinct from ordinary legislation) was first asserted in Kesavananda and consolidated in Minerva Mills.
• The case involved nationalisation of Minerva Mills Ltd. under the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act, 1974.

solution.concept_anchor: I.R. Coelho — basic structure test for post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know 'Ninth Schedule provides immunity' may select option (a), failing to appreciate that the immunity is conditional on the basic structure test for post-1973 additions.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Ninth Schedule immunity is not absolute for all laws — post-1973 additions are open to challenge; this was precisely the ruling in I.R. Coelho.
Eliminate option (b): I.R. Coelho was a nine-judge bench, not a seven-judge bench — and it did not hold that the Ninth Schedule is unconstitutional.

Eliminate option (d): The test in I.R. Coelho is not merely whether the law violates Article 14 or 19 separately; it is whether the law damages basic structure including core FRs under 14, 19, and 21.

Retain option (c): I.R. Coelho held that laws added to the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 are open to challenge on basic structure grounds, and FRs under Articles 14, 19, 21 form part of basic structure.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the assumption that placement in the Ninth Schedule provides absolute immunity from judicial review. I.R. Coelho (2007) clarified that this immunity is temporal — only pre-April 24, 1973 additions enjoy unconditional immunity. The case elevated the status of FRs under Articles 14, 19, and 21 by making them components of the basic structure that post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws cannot abridge.
solution.final_explanation:
I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) is the most authoritative pronouncement on the limits of Ninth Schedule immunity.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: I.R. Coelho explicitly held that Ninth Schedule immunity is not absolute. Laws placed there after the Kesavananda date (April 24, 1973) can be challenged.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The bench in I.R. Coelho consisted of nine judges. The ruling did not declare the Ninth Schedule itself unconstitutional — it clarified the scope of its immunity.
• Option (c) — Correct: The nine-judge bench held that laws added to the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 are subject to judicial review on basic structure grounds, and FRs under Articles 14, 19, and 21 are basic structure elements that such laws cannot damage.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The test is not whether the law violates Article 14 or 19 in isolation, but whether it damages the basic structure, which includes core FRs as identified in the case.

Value Addition:
• The Waman Rao (1981) ruling established the April 24, 1973 cutoff; I.R. Coelho (2007) refined and strengthened it.
• Over 280 laws are currently listed in the Ninth Schedule, predominantly land reform and reservation statutes.
• The Tamil Nadu law at issue in I.R. Coelho provided 69% reservation — among the highest in any state.

solution.concept_anchor: 42nd Amendment — what it attempted vs what courts invalidated
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who recall Minerva Mills struck down the 42nd Amendment's DPSP provisions may assume the entire Amendment was invalidated, including Fundamental Duties.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs — not Article 31C itself — was struck down; the original Article 31C covering Articles 39(b)/(c) survives.
Eliminate option (b): Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) added by the 42nd Amendment were not struck down by Minerva Mills — they remain constitutionally valid.
Eliminate option (c): Minerva Mills struck down the 42nd Amendment's DPSP-related provisions; it did not reverse all the Amendment's additions — new DPSPs and Fundamental Duties survived.

Retain option (d): The correctly targeted invalidation was the explicit attempt to subordinate Articles 14 and 19 to all DPSPs by extending Article 31C — this was the 42nd Amendment's provision that Minerva Mills held unconstitutional.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students conflate 'the 42nd Amendment's DPSP-related provisions were struck down' with 'the entire 42nd Amendment was invalidated.' Minerva Mills surgically struck down the extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs and the ouster of judicial review — it left untouched the new DPSPs added to Part IV and the Fundamental Duties in Part IVA. This precision is the exam trap.
solution.final_explanation:
A law review committee must advise Parliament on which specific provision of the 42nd Amendment was invalidated by Minerva Mills (1980).

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The original Article 31C (covering Articles 39(b) and 39(c)) was upheld in Kesavananda and was never struck down. Minerva Mills struck down only its extension to all DPSPs.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Fundamental Duties under Article 51A are constitutionally valid. Minerva Mills did not address them — they were not the basis for the DPSP supremacy challenge.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Minerva Mills did not invalidate the new DPSPs added to Part IV by the 42nd Amendment (such as Article 48A on environment). These survive as valid DPSPs.
• Option (d) — Correct: The precise invalidation by Minerva Mills was the 42nd Amendment's clause extending Article 31C to all DPSPs, which attempted to subordinate Articles 14 and 19 to every DPSP. This clause violated the basic structure by destroying the constitutional balance between FRs and DPSPs.

Value Addition:
• The 42nd Amendment also added Article 31D on anti-national activities — this was repealed by the 44th Amendment (1978), not by Minerva Mills.
• Post-Minerva Mills, Article 31C remains in force but only for Articles 39(b) and (c) — its original scope.
• Minerva Mills also struck down the 42nd Amendment's clause excluding judicial review of constitutional amendments — a separate holding from the Article 31C ruling.

solution.concept_anchor: Founding vision of FRs and DPSPs as complementary

statement_analysis.statement: In the Constituent Assembly debates, Dr B.R. Ambedkar envisioned Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles as complementary instruments of social transformation, not as adversarial provisions.
statement_analysis.reason: Ambedkar, along with Nehru, consistently presented FRs and DPSPs as mutually reinforcing — political and civil rights alongside social and economic objectives of governance.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 37 expressly declares that Directive Principles are enforceable in courts of law in the same manner as Fundamental Rights under Part III.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 37 expressly states the opposite — DPSPs are 'not enforceable by any court,' distinguishing them clearly from the justiciable Fundamental Rights.

statement_analysis.statement: The original constitutional text treats Part IV (Directive Principles) as superior to Part III (Fundamental Rights) in the event of legislative conflict.
statement_analysis.reason: The original Constitution's text contains no explicit supremacy clause for DPSPs over FRs. The Champakam ruling (1951) confirmed that FRs prevail — leading to First Amendment changes.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Champakam established FR supremacy may infer the original text must have been silent or ambiguous, leading them to reject Statement 3 on different grounds but also doubt Statement 1.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Ambedkar and Nehru's Constituent Assembly speeches consistently framed FRs and DPSPs as complementary pillars.
Statement 2 is incorrect — Article 37 explicitly states DPSPs are 'not enforceable by any court,' the opposite of what the statement claims.
Statement 3 is incorrect — the original Constitution contained no DPSP supremacy clause; Champakam confirmed FR primacy existed by implication.
Only Statement 1 is correct → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 directly exploits students who may confuse 'fundamental to governance' (Article 37's actual language) with 'enforceable in courts.' Article 37 uses both phrases but they are logically distinct — something can be fundamental to governance without being court-enforceable. Statement 3 exploits the assumption that because later amendments and cases established a hierarchy, the original Constitution must have had one explicitly.
solution.final_explanation:
The founding constitutional vision of the DPSP–FR relationship differs from the adversarial characterisation that emerged in practice.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Ambedkar described DPSPs as 'instruments of instruction' to governments and presented them as the economic-social complement to the political freedoms in Part III. The adversarial framing was a product of litigation, not founding intent.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 37 expressly declares DPSPs 'not enforceable by any court,' making them non-justiciable. The phrase 'fundamental to governance' in Article 37 denotes political salience, not legal enforceability.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: No explicit DPSP supremacy clause existed in the original Constitution. The first major judicial interpretation (Champakam, 1951) confirmed that FRs were textually and structurally superior, which prompted the First Amendment to correct this through Article 15(4).

Value Addition:
• The Irish Constitution of 1937 served as a model for India's DPSPs — Ireland similarly made them non-justiciable.
• Nehru described DPSPs as 'the soul of the Constitution,' emphasising their political weight despite non-justiciability.
• The tension between original intent (complementary) and judicial practice (conflict) is the defining theme of the DPSP–FR relationship.

solution.concept_anchor: Constitutional amendments enabling educational reservations — case and amendment mapping
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who conflate the PA Inamdar ruling (which restricted reservation in private unaided institutions) with the TMA Pai ruling (which created the regulation hierarchy) may swap B and C.
elimination_logic: A (Champakam Dorairajan, 1951) → directly triggered the First Constitutional Amendment's addition of Article 15(4): matches description 4.
B (PA Inamdar, 2005) → held that unaided private institutions cannot be compelled to provide reservation: matches description 2.
C (93rd Amendment, 2005) → Parliamentary response to PA Inamdar, inserted Article 15(5) enabling reservation in private unaided institutions (with Article 30 exception): matches description 1.
D (TMA Pai Foundation, 2002) → established the regulatory hierarchy: minority unaided > non-minority unaided > aided institutions: matches description 3.
Correct combination: A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3 → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The PA Inamdar and TMA Pai cases are the most commonly confused pair in this cluster. TMA Pai established the hierarchy of permissible state regulation, while PA Inamdar applied that hierarchy to hold that unaided private institutions cannot be subjected to reservation mandates. Swapping their holdings is the classic exam trap — options (a) and (b) are designed to exploit this confusion.
solution.final_explanation:
The evolution of reservation in educational institutions spans judicial pronouncements and parliamentary responses.

Correct Matching:
• A (Champakam Dorairajan, 1951) → 4: The case established FR supremacy over DPSPs and directly led to the First Amendment adding Article 15(4) for backward classes.
• B (PA Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra, 2005) → 2: Held that unaided private institutions — minority and non-minority — cannot be compelled to implement state reservation policies.
• C (93rd Constitutional Amendment, 2005) → 1: Parliament's response to PA Inamdar — inserted Article 15(5) enabling reservation in private unaided institutions, with an express proviso excluding minority institutions under Article 30.
• D (TMA Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka, 2002) → 3: Established the three-tier regulatory hierarchy based on institution type and funding.

Value Addition:
• Article 15(5) explicitly excepts minority educational institutions established under Article 30 — a critical constitutional protection.
• Both TMA Pai and PA Inamdar were decided by 11-judge constitutional benches — among the largest in Indian judicial history on this subject.
• The 93rd Amendment is a textbook example of Parliament amending an FR (Article 15) to accommodate a DPSP goal (Article 41 — right to education for weaker sections).

solution.concept_anchor: Shah Bano case — Article 44 invocation and legislative reversal

statement_analysis.statement: In the Shah Bano case (1985), the Supreme Court awarded maintenance to a divorced Muslim woman and explicitly invoked Article 44 urging Parliament to enact a Uniform Civil Code.
statement_analysis.reason: The Shah Bano ruling both awarded maintenance under the Code of Criminal Procedure (Section 125) and expressly invoked Article 44 as a constitutional aspiration Parliament should fulfil.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament's response to the Shah Bano judgment was to enact the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, which codified the Supreme Court's ruling and extended maintenance rights beyond the iddat period.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1986 Act was enacted specifically to override the Shah Bano ruling — it restricted maintenance to the iddat period and removed divorced Muslim women from the scope of Section 125 CrPC, reversing the judgment.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court in Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) reiterated the call for a Uniform Civil Code but held that the personal laws of different religious communities are protected by Article 25 and cannot be legislatively altered.
statement_analysis.reason: Sarla Mudgal did urge Parliament on UCC but did NOT hold that personal laws are constitutionally immune from legislative alteration. Article 25(2)(b) permits regulation of secular activities associated with religion.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the 1986 Act overrode Shah Bano may accept Statement 2 as correct if they misread 'codified the ruling' versus 'reversed the ruling,' and may overlook the Statement 3 error entirely.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Shah Bano awarded maintenance and invoked Article 44.
Statement 2 is incorrect — the 1986 Act reversed, not codified, the Shah Bano ruling by restricting maintenance to the iddat period.
Statement 3 is incorrect — Sarla Mudgal did not hold personal laws immune from legislative change; Article 25(2)(b) expressly permits regulation of secular aspects of religion.
Statements 2 and 3 are incorrect → option (c) — verify option letters in display text.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a partial-truth trap: students who know the 1986 Act was Parliament's 'response' to Shah Bano may not catch that 'codified and extended' is the opposite of what happened — the Act curtailed maintenance rights. Statement 3 appears authoritative but falsely attributes an absolute immunity holding to Sarla Mudgal, which the case never said. Both wrongs require precise case knowledge to identify.
solution.final_explanation:
The Shah Bano controversy illustrates the political volatility of the UCC debate and Parliament's capacity to override Supreme Court rulings through legislation.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Shah Bano (1985) awarded maintenance under Section 125 CrPC and explicitly called upon Parliament to fulfil the Article 44 directive by enacting a UCC.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 did not codify or extend the Shah Bano ruling — it reversed it. The Act confined maintenance to the iddat period and excluded divorced Muslim women from Section 125 CrPC's scope.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Sarla Mudgal (1995) urged Parliament on UCC but made no holding that personal laws enjoy absolute constitutional protection. Article 25(2)(b) explicitly permits the state to regulate secular activities associated with religion — personal law reform falls within this power.

Value Addition:
• John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003) further reiterated the UCC call, specifically challenging Section 118 of the Indian Succession Act's discriminatory provisions.
• The Supreme Court's UCC calls are advisory, not binding — only Parliament can enact a UCC.
• Article 44 is classified among the 'Gandhian principles' group by some scholars, though the UCC itself was Nehru's broader civil modernisation goal.
