solution.concept_anchor: Article 300A enforcement through Article 226 not Article 32
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Article 32 as the 'right to constitutional remedies' may instinctively complete the blank with 'Article 32' without checking whether Article 300A qualifies as a Fundamental Right.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Article 32 enforces Fundamental Rights listed in Part III — Article 300A is in Part XII and is not a FR.
Eliminate option (c): Article 136 is the Supreme Court's special leave jurisdiction — it is not a writ remedy for rights violations.
Eliminate option (d): Article 226 jurisdiction is for High Courts — but a person deprived of property under Article 300A must approach the High Court under 226, not a lower court.
Retain option (b): The correct remedy for Article 300A violation is a writ petition to the High Court under Article 226, since Article 300A is not a FR and Article 32 does not apply.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The instinctive answer for any constitutional rights violation is Article 32 (Supreme Court writ jurisdiction). The trap requires students to recognise that Article 300A is NOT a Fundamental Right — it is a legal/constitutional right in Part XII. Article 32 is the 'right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights' — it does not cover Part XII rights. Only the broader writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 (which covers not just FRs but 'any other purpose') can address Article 300A violations.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 300A creates a legal right — not a Fundamental Right — and the choice of remedy follows from this classification.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Article 32 grants the Supreme Court jurisdiction to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights in Part III. Article 300A is in Part XII — it is not a FR, so Article 32 is unavailable.
• Option (b) — Correct: Article 226 grants High Courts broad writ jurisdiction extending beyond Fundamental Rights to 'any other purpose.' A person deprived of property without legal authority under Article 300A must approach the High Court under Article 226.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) is an appellate power of the Supreme Court — it is not a primary remedy for rights violations.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Civil courts may adjudicate property disputes but are not the constitutional remedy for Article 300A violations; the appropriate constitutional remedy is a High Court writ.

Value Addition:
• The practical significance: a person whose property is taken without legal authority cannot file a writ petition in the Supreme Court directly under Article 32.
• Article 226's broader scope — 'any other purpose' — makes High Courts the constitutional guardians for non-FR rights like Article 300A.
• Post-44th Amendment, the absence of Article 19(1)(f) also means the 'reasonable restriction' standard no longer applies to property deprivation — only 'legal authority' is required.

solution.concept_anchor: 25th Amendment Article 31C — correct year and FRs it overrides
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who recall Article 31C protects laws from Articles 14, 19 AND 21 challenges may select option (b) — but Article 31C's shield does not extend to Article 21.
elimination_logic: Examine option (a): The 25th Amendment was enacted in 1971, not 1969 — temporal-swap makes this incorrect.
Examine option (b): Article 31C protects laws from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, NOT Article 21 — scope-extension makes the pair incorrect.
Examine option (c): Article 31C as currently operative protects only Articles 39(b) and 39(c), not all DPSPs — Minerva Mills struck down the extension to all DPSPs.
Examine option (d): Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971) to shield laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19 — this pair is correctly stated.
Option (d) is the correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) exploits a critical scope error: students who know Article 31C provides a shield from FR challenges may assume it covers Article 21 (right to life) as well. In fact, Article 31C specifically and only shields from Articles 14 and 19 challenges — laws implementing Articles 39(b)/(c) can still be challenged under Article 21. This distinction has significant practical implications for property and nationalisation legislation.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 31C is one of the most precisely worded provisions in the constitutional text — knowing exactly what it covers and what it does not is essential.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The 25th Amendment was enacted in 1971, not 1969. A two-year temporal swap.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Article 31C shields laws from challenge under Articles 14 and 19 only — not Article 21. A law implementing Articles 39(b)/(c) can still be challenged on right-to-life grounds.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Post-Minerva Mills (1980), Article 31C protects only laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) — not all DPSPs. The extension to all DPSPs was struck down.
• Option (d) — Correct: Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971). In its current operative form (post-Minerva Mills), it shields laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.

Value Addition:
• Article 21 is conspicuously absent from Article 31C's shield — this is intentional; the right to life and personal liberty was considered an absolute minimum not to be subordinated.
• Kesavananda (1973) struck down Article 31C's non-justiciability clause but upheld its protective shield.
• The 25th Amendment also substituted 'amount' for 'compensation' in Article 31(2), removing the requirement of equivalent compensation for property acquisition.

solution.concept_anchor: Landmark DPSP–FR cases in correct chronological sequence
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who recall the 'Champakam → Kesavananda → Minerva Mills' sequence but misplace Waman Rao (often confused with post-Minerva Mills Coelho cases) may invert the last two.
elimination_logic: Champakam Dorairajan (1951) is the earliest — the first FR-DPSP conflict ruling.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) came next — establishing the basic structure doctrine and reconciliation formula.
Minerva Mills (1980) followed — applying and refining Kesavananda to strike down the 42nd Amendment's DPSP extension.
Waman Rao (1981) came after Minerva Mills — applying the Kesavananda date (April 24, 1973) to determine Ninth Schedule immunity.
Correct order: Champakam (1951) → Kesavananda (1973) → Minerva Mills (1980) → Waman Rao (1981) → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Waman Rao (1981) is the least-memorised case in this cluster and is frequently displaced in sequencing questions. Students who know it postdates Kesavananda may place it before Minerva Mills (1980), not realising both Minerva Mills and Waman Rao came after Kesavananda. Options are designed to test whether students know the precise year-gap between these cases.
solution.final_explanation:
The chronological sequence of landmark DPSP–FR cases maps the evolution from conflict to constitutional reconciliation.

• Champakam Dorairajan (1951): First case establishing FR supremacy — the starting point of the conflict.
• Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Basic structure doctrine — Parliament can amend FRs for DPSPs but cannot destroy constitutional fundamentals; April 24, 1973 becomes the constitutional dividing line.
• Minerva Mills (1980): Applied Kesavananda — struck down the 42nd Amendment's DPSP-supremacy provisions; affirmed judicial review as basic structure.
• Waman Rao (1981): Applied the Kesavananda date — pre-1973 Ninth Schedule laws enjoy full FR immunity; post-1973 additions are reviewable.

Wrong options either place Waman Rao before Minerva Mills or invert Kesavananda and Champakam.

Value Addition:
• All four cases together form the essential 'DPSP–FR jurisprudence' arc that UPSC tests as a coherent whole.
• I.R. Coelho (2007) is the fifth landmark — a nine-judge bench elaboration on the Waman Rao cutoff.
• The sequence also tracks the evolution of the basic structure doctrine from assertion (Kesavananda) to consolidation (Minerva Mills) to application (Waman Rao).

solution.concept_anchor: Article 19(6) public interest restriction read with Article 39(b)
solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who recall Article 31C provides a shield for Article 39(b)-implementing laws may assume it automatically applies whenever Article 39(b) is invoked, without checking whether Articles 14 and 19 are the challenged provisions.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Article 31C is the relevant provision for shielding laws implementing Articles 39(b)/(c) from Articles 14 and 19 challenges — but the precise mechanism by which courts sustain Article 19(1)(g) restrictions is by reading Article 19(6)'s 'public interest' ground with DPSP objectives.

Identify option (b): Article 19(6) permits restrictions on trade/profession 'in the interests of the general public' — courts read DPSP objectives like Article 39(b) into 'general public interest' to sustain nationalisation restrictions.
Eliminate option (c): The doctrine of harmonious construction applies to interpretive conflicts, not directly to the mechanism by which Article 19(6) restrictions are validated.

Eliminate option (d): Article 31C provides a shield from Articles 14 and 19 challenges — it operates by exempting the law from these articles entirely, not by finding a restriction ground within Article 19(6); these are two different analytical routes.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The confusion between Article 31C and Article 19(6) is the trap. Article 31C eliminates the need to justify a restriction under Article 19 by simply exempting the law from Article 19's scrutiny. Article 19(6), by contrast, is the mechanism by which a restriction survives Article 19 scrutiny — courts read DPSP objectives into 'public interest' under 19(6). These are different routes to the same outcome, and confusing them leads to a wrong answer. The scenario specifies a restriction 'upheld as reasonable' — pointing to Article 19(6), not Article 31C immunity.
solution.final_explanation:
A state government nationalises private bus services. The affected operators challenge the law under Article 19(1)(g) (right to trade). The state justifies it by citing Article 39(b)'s directive on distribution of material resources.

The constitutional mechanism at work here is Article 19(6) — the 'public interest' restriction ground within Article 19 itself:

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Article 31C provides a complete shield from Article 19 scrutiny for laws implementing Articles 39(b)/(c) — but the scenario describes a court assessing 'reasonableness,' which occurs under Article 19(6), not under Article 31C's immunity route.
• Option (b) — Correct: Courts read the DPSP objective of Article 39(b) — distributing material resources for the common good — into Article 19(6)'s 'interests of the general public' ground, thereby sustaining the restriction on the right to run a trade or business.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Harmonious construction is an interpretive principle, not the direct constitutional mechanism for validating Article 19 restrictions.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Article 31C exempts qualifying laws from Article 19 challenges altogether — it does not operate within the Article 19(6) reasonableness framework.

Value Addition:
• State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy (1977) addressed this precise scenario — nationalisation of private bus services was challenged under Article 19(1)(g).
• Article 19(6) also permits state monopoly of any trade or business — an independent ground for nationalisation.
• DPSP objectives functioning as the 'public interest' content of Article 19(6) is a common UPSC examination pattern.

solution.concept_anchor: Fundamental Duties — non-justiciable but used to assess FR restriction reasonableness
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify both A and R as true may automatically select (a) without carefully testing whether the causal relationship holds — whether FDs being non-justiciable specifically explains their use to assess FR restriction reasonableness.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. Courts have used Article 51A to assess whether a restriction on an FR is reasonable — AIIMS Students' Union v. AIIMS (2002) confirms this.
Step 2: Is R correct? — Yes. Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable, like DPSPs — this is the clear constitutional position under Part IVA.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. A says courts USE FDs to assess FR reasonableness; R says FDs are non-justiciable. These two facts are independent — non-justiciability does not cause or explain the interpretive usage. If anything, the interpretive use is despite non-justiciability, not because of it. R does not logically explain A.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → correct option is (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between Fundamental Duties and Fundamental Rights mirrors the DPSPs–FRs relationship in an important structural way.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: Courts have used Article 51A obligations to assess whether a restriction on an FR is 'reasonable.' In AIIMS Students' Union v. AIIMS (2002), the Supreme Court held that FDs, while non-justiciable, can be invoked to determine the constitutional reasonableness of state action that limits FRs where citizens are violating their duties.
• Reason (R) — Correct: Fundamental Duties are indeed non-justiciable — no court can compel their performance through a writ petition, just as DPSPs cannot be directly enforced.
• Causal Link — Absent: R describes the legal status of FDs (non-justiciable) but does not explain why or how they can be used to assess FR restriction reasonableness. The interpretive use of FDs occurs despite their non-justiciability, not because of it. R is a factually true but causally disconnected statement relative to A.

Value Addition:
• Article 51A(g) — duty to protect the environment — is most frequently used by courts alongside Article 48A DPSP and Article 21 to assess environmental restrictions.
• Fundamental Duties were recommended by the Swaran Singh Committee (1976) and added by the 42nd Amendment.
• India's 11 Fundamental Duties are modelled partly on Article 29(1) of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which acknowledges duties to the community.

solution.concept_anchor: Pre and post-44th Amendment property rights constitutional landscape

statement_analysis.statement: Prior to the 44th Amendment, the right to property was a Fundamental Right under both Article 19(1)(f) (freedom to acquire and hold property) and Article 31 (protection against deprivation without compensation).
statement_analysis.reason: Before the 44th Amendment (1978), property was protected as a FR through two distinct provisions — Article 19(1)(f) (right to hold property) and Article 31 (right against arbitrary acquisition).

statement_analysis.statement: The 44th Amendment's deletion of Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 means that no constitutional protection for property rights exists post-1978 — only ordinary statutory laws protect property.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 300A, inserted by the 44th Amendment, provides constitutional protection — it requires legal authority for any deprivation of property. Constitutional protection exists, only shifted from Part III to Part XII.

statement_analysis.statement: After the deletion of Article 19(1)(f), a law restricting the use or acquisition of property need not satisfy the 'reasonable restriction' standard applicable under Article 19 — it only requires legal authority under Article 300A.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 19's restriction framework (reasonableness, proportionality under clauses 2–6) no longer applies to property post-44th Amendment. Article 300A only requires 'authority of law' — a lower constitutional threshold.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as correct may second-guess Statement 1 if they recall the Ninth Schedule or other property-related provisions, making option (b) (1 only) seem cautiously safe.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — pre-1978, property was a FR under both Articles 19(1)(f) and 31.
Statement 2 is incorrect — Article 300A provides constitutional (though not FR) protection for property; it is not mere statutory protection.
Statement 3 is correct — post-44th Amendment, the 'reasonable restriction' standard of Article 19 does not apply to property; only 'authority of law' under Article 300A is required.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the common assumption that removing a Fundamental Right eliminates all constitutional protection. Article 300A is a constitutional provision — it requires an Act of Parliament or Legislature, not merely an executive order, for property deprivation. The protection is real, though weaker than a FR (no Article 32 remedy; no 'reasonableness' standard). Students who conflate 'not a FR' with 'no constitutional protection' will accept Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The 44th Amendment's deletion of Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 fundamentally altered the constitutional landscape for property rights and DPSP accommodation.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The original Constitution protected property through two distinct provisions — Article 19(1)(f) (acquisition and holding) and Article 31 (compensation for compulsory acquisition). Both were deleted by the 44th Amendment.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Property retains constitutional protection under Article 300A (Part XII). The state must still act under legal authority — an executive fiat without legislative backing violates Article 300A. The protection is reduced, not eliminated.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 'reasonable restriction' analysis under Article 19 required proportionality, nexus with permissible grounds, and judicial scrutiny. Under Article 300A, the sole test is whether the deprivation is backed by an Act of law — a significantly lower bar.

Value Addition:
• Article 300A deprivation by mere executive order (without an Act) is unconstitutional — this is the residual constitutional protection.
• Post-44th Amendment, DPSPs on material resources (Articles 39(b)/(c)) face far less constitutional resistance — the central tension zone moved to administrative law.
• Article 300A was upheld as a valid constitutional right in Jilubhai v. State of Gujarat (1995).

solution.concept_anchor: Landmark DPSP–FR reconciliation mechanisms — correctly paired

statement_analysis.statement: Champakam Dorairajan (1951) established that when a Directive Principle and a Fundamental Right conflict, courts must attempt harmonious construction before declaring FR supremacy.
statement_analysis.reason: Champakam established FR supremacy directly without articulating a harmonious construction requirement. Harmonious construction as the preferred approach was developed later in cases like Pathumma v. State of Kerala (1978).

statement_analysis.statement: Article 31C, in its post-Minerva Mills form, provides that no law giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) shall be void on the ground that it is inconsistent with the rights conferred by Articles 14 and 19.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the operative scope of Article 31C — the shield covers Articles 39(b)/(c) implementing laws from Articles 14 and 19 challenges. The extension to all DPSPs was struck down.

statement_analysis.statement: The basic structure doctrine, as articulated in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), holds that while Parliament may amend Fundamental Rights to implement Directive Principles, the harmony between Part III and Part IV is itself a component of the basic structure.
statement_analysis.reason: Kesavananda held that Parliament has the amending power for FRs vis-à-vis DPSPs but cannot destroy the basic structure — and Minerva Mills later clarified that the Part III–Part IV balance is itself basic structure.

statement_analysis.statement: In Minerva Mills (1980), the Supreme Court held that Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is unlimited, provided the amendment serves a Directive Principle objective.
statement_analysis.reason: Minerva Mills held the precise opposite — Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is limited by the basic structure doctrine regardless of the objective. No DPSP purpose can override this limitation.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who correctly identify Statement 3 as correct and reject Statement 4 but are uncertain about Statements 1 and 2 may guess 'Only three' by accepting Statement 1 as a reasonable inference.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect — Champakam established outright FR supremacy, not harmonious construction as the first step.
Statement 2 is correct — Article 31C in its current form protects Articles 39(b)/(c)-implementing laws from Articles 14 and 19 challenges.
Statement 3 is correct — Kesavananda permitted FR amendments for DPSP implementation within basic structure limits; Minerva Mills added that the balance itself is basic structure.
Statement 4 is incorrect — Minerva Mills explicitly rejected unlimited amending power and struck down the 42nd Amendment's DPSP-supremacy provisions.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct — 'Only two' → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 carefully attributes the 'Part III–Part IV balance as basic structure' to Kesavananda, when more precisely this articulation comes from Minerva Mills. The statement is not wrong, because Kesavananda's general basic structure finding can logically encompass it, but students who know Minerva Mills specifically articulated this principle may doubt Statement 3's attribution and incorrectly mark it incorrect. This makes the 'Only two' count harder to confirm.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests comprehensive understanding of the DPSP–FR reconciliation mechanisms across cases and provisions.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Champakam (1951) directly declared FR supremacy — it did not require harmonious construction as a precondition. That principle developed separately in later jurisprudence.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Post-Minerva Mills, Article 31C shields only laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) from Articles 14 and 19 challenges. This is the operative constitutional text.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Kesavananda established that Parliament can amend FRs for DPSP implementation within basic structure limits. Minerva Mills later crystalised that the Part III–Part IV balance is itself a basic structure element.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Minerva Mills categorically rejected unlimited amending power. Parliament cannot abrogate basic structure elements even when pursuing legitimate DPSP objectives.

Value Addition:
• The intersection of Kesavananda + Minerva Mills creates the governing formula: Parliament may balance FRs and DPSPs but may not destroy either.
• Article 31C does not shield laws from Article 21 challenges — a frequently overlooked limitation.
• Statements 2 and 3, taken together, describe the current equilibrium: limited Article 31C shield + basic structure ceiling on amendments.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 15(5) exception for minority institutions under Article 30
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who recall that TMA Pai (2002) was decided before PA Inamdar (2005) may conflate their holdings and misidentify TMA Pai as not belonging to the 'educational reservation' cluster.
elimination_logic: PA Inamdar (2005) held that unaided private institutions cannot be subjected to state reservation — directly in the educational reservation cluster.
93rd Constitutional Amendment (2005) inserted Article 15(5) enabling reservation in private unaided institutions — directly in the cluster.
TMA Pai Foundation (2002) established the regulatory hierarchy for educational institutions — directly in the educational institution regulation cluster.

Article 15(3) concerns special provisions for women and children — it predates the entire educational reservation debate and was part of the original Constitution, with no connection to private unaided institution reservation.
Article 15(3) is the odd one out → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap: Article 15(3), Article 15(4), and Article 15(5) are all sub-clauses of Article 15, making them appear to belong together. However, Article 15(3) (special provisions for women and children) has nothing to do with educational reservation or the private-institution debate — it was in the original Constitution for a different purpose. Article 15(5) is the relevant reservation provision, and Article 15(4) (backward classes) is its earlier cousin from the First Amendment. Grouping them all as 'Article 15 provisions' obscures the functional distinction.
solution.final_explanation:
Three of these four entries share a direct connection to the constitutional debate over reservation in private unaided educational institutions.

• PA Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005): Held that private unaided institutions — minority and non-minority alike — cannot be compelled to follow state reservation policy. Directly in the cluster.
• 93rd Constitutional Amendment (2005): Parliament's direct response — inserted Article 15(5) to enable reservation in private unaided institutions, with an Article 30 exception for minority institutions. Directly in the cluster.
• TMA Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002): Established the foundational three-tier hierarchy of regulatory power over educational institutions. Directly in the cluster.
• Article 15(3): Enables special provisions for women and children — it was part of the original Constitution (1950) and has no connection to the private institution reservation debate. It is the odd one out.

Value Addition:
• Article 15(4) — backward class reservation — added by the First Amendment (1951) is the cousin of Article 15(5) but serves a different purpose.
• Article 15(5) was constitutionally challenged but upheld by the Supreme Court in Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India (2008).
• The Article 30 exception in Article 15(5) is the constitutional safeguard ensuring minority educational autonomy.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Article 48A is one of the new DPSPs added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) — along with Articles 39A (free legal aid), 43A (worker participation in management), and 48A (environment). Students who encounter Article 48A in environmental cases may assume it is part of the foundational constitutional text. The original Constitution's DPSPs did not include environmental protection — this was a 1976 addition responding to the Stockholm Conference (1972) and growing environmental awareness.
solution.final_explanation:
Environmental rights under Article 21 rest on a DPSP provision that itself was not present at the Constitution's inception.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991) established that the right to live in an environment free from pollution is a component of the right to life under Article 21, derived by reading Article 21 with Article 48A (DPSP on state's duty to protect environment).
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 48A is not part of the original Constitution. It was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976) as a new Directive Principle — one of several environmental and social justice provisions added during the Emergency period.

Value Addition:
• Article 48A mandates that the state shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wildlife of the country.
• The Stockholm Declaration (1972) on the Human Environment significantly influenced the addition of Article 48A.
• The MC Mehta series of cases (beginning in the 1980s) built extensively on Article 48A + Article 21 to develop India's environmental jurisprudence — including the Polluter Pays Principle and Precautionary Principle.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know basic structure and harmonious construction as linked doctrines may swap their descriptions, particularly since both are 'balancing' approaches.
elimination_logic: A (Harmonious Construction) → The principle that courts read FRs and DPSPs together to find a mutually consistent interpretation before declaring irreconcilable conflict: matches description 3.
B (Basic Structure Doctrine) → The constitutional ceiling on Parliament's amending power — DPSPs cannot be implemented by destroying constitutional fundamentals: matches description 1.

C (Article 31C Legislative Shield) → Parliamentary instrument shielding laws implementing specific DPSPs (39(b)/(c)) from Articles 14 and 19 challenges, without requiring judicial resolution: matches description 4.

Correct: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Conflation between harmonious construction (a judicial interpretive technique) and the basic structure doctrine (a constitutional amendment limitation) is the primary trap. Both involve 'balancing' but operate at different levels — harmonious construction is applied to ordinary legislation; the basic structure doctrine governs constitutional amendments. Swapping their descriptions produces options (c) and (d), which are the designed distractors.
solution.final_explanation:
Four distinct mechanisms govern the DPSP–FR relationship — they operate at different institutional levels and must not be conflated.

Correct Matching:
• A (Harmonious Construction) → 3: Courts' default interpretive approach — reading FRs and DPSPs together to find a mutually consistent meaning, avoiding a declaration of irreconcilable conflict wherever possible.
• B (Basic Structure Doctrine) → 1: Kesavananda's constraint on Parliament — DPSPs can motivate FR amendments but cannot be used to destroy the fundamental constitutional framework. Applied to constitutional amendments, not ordinary legislation.
• C (Article 31C Legislative Shield) → 4: A Parliamentary instrument (not a judicial doctrine) that pre-emptively removes qualifying DPSP-implementing laws from Articles 14 and 19 scrutiny.
• D (Article 37 Non-justiciability) → 2: The constitutional text's own declaration — DPSPs are binding governance directives but courts cannot be petitioned to enforce them through writs.

Value Addition:
• The four mechanisms form a hierarchy: harmonious construction (first resort) → reasonable restriction reading of Article 19 → Article 31C shield → basic structure ceiling on amendments.
• Non-justiciability (Article 37) is a textual rule; harmonious construction is a judicial doctrine built on top of it.
• Article 31C's legislative shield is unique — it operates ex ante (before litigation) rather than through judicial determination.
